<article class="ltx_document ltx_authors_1line">
<h1 class="ltx_title ltx_font_bold ltx_title_document">Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures<span class="ltx_pubnotes"><span class="ltx_pubnotes_content"><span class="ltx_pubnote ltx_role_thanks"><span class="ltx_note_name">Thanks: </span><span id="id1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Songrun He is at Washington University in St. Louis (<a href="mailto:h.songrun@wustl.edu" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter ltx_font_medium">h.songrun@wustl.edu</a>). Asaf Manela is at Washington University in St. Louis and Reichman University (<a href="mailto:amanela@wustl.edu" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter ltx_font_medium">amanela@wustl.edu</a>). Omri Ross is at University of Copenhagen (<a href="mailto:omri@di.ku.dk" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter ltx_font_medium">omri@di.ku.dk</a>), and Chief Blockchain Scientist at the eToro Group. Victor von Wachter is at University of Copenhagen (<a href="mailto:victor.vonwachter@di.ku.dk" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter ltx_font_medium">victor.vonwachter@di.ku.dk</a>).</span></span></span></span></h1>
<div class="ltx_authors">
<span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Songrun He
</span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Asaf Manela
</span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Omri Ross
</span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Victor von Wachter
</span></span></div>
<div class="ltx_dates">January 2023</div>

<div id="p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="p1.1" class="ltx_p ltx_align_center"><span id="p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Abstract</span></p>
</div>
<div id="p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="p2.1" class="ltx_p">Perpetual futures—swap contracts that never expire—are by far the most popular derivative traded in cryptocurrency markets, with more than $100 billion traded daily.
Perpetuals provide investors with leveraged exposure to cryptocurrencies, which does not require rollover or direct cryptocurrency holding.
To keep the gap between perpetual futures and spot prices small, long position holders periodically pay short position holders a funding rate proportional to this gap. The funding rate incentivizes trades that tend to narrow the futures-spot gap.
But unlike fixed-maturity futures, perpetuals are not guaranteed to converge to the spot price of their underlying asset at any time, and familiar no-arbitrage prices for perpetuals are not available, as the contracts have no expiry date to enforce arbitrage.
Here, using a weaker notion of random-maturity arbitrage, we derive no-arbitrage prices for perpetual futures in frictionless markets and no-arbitrage bounds for markets with trading costs.
These no-arbitrage prices provide a valuable benchmark for perpetual futures and simultaneously prescribe a strategy to exploit divergence from these fundamental values.
Empirically, we find that deviations of crypto perpetual futures from no-arbitrage prices are considerably larger than those documented in traditional currency markets. These deviations comove across cryptocurrencies and diminish over time as crypto markets develop and become more efficient. A simple trading strategy generates large Sharpe ratios even for investors paying the highest trading costs on Binance, which is currently the largest crypto exchange by volume.
<span id="p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">JEL Classification</span>: G11, G12, G13 
<br class="ltx_break"><span id="p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Keywords</span>: Perpetual Futures, Crypto, Arbitrage, Funding Rate</p>
</div>
<div class="ltx_pagination ltx_role_newpage"></div>
<section id="S1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">1 </span>Introduction</h2>

<div id="S1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Perpetual futures are by far the most popular derivative traded in cryptocurrency markets, generating a daily volume of more than $100 billion.
Before the recent collapse of FTX, perpetual futures were among the most actively-traded products on the exchange, with the now bankrupt hedge fund Alameda Research taking the other side of many such leveraged trades. Despite their central role in crypto markets, there is relatively little work studying these derivatives. In this paper we ask, what are the fundamental values of perpetual futures theoretically, and how large are deviations from these fundamentals empirically?</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Perpetuals are an efficient vehicle for investors to hedge and speculate on cryptocurrencies with high leverage, without necessarily taking delivery of cryptocurrencies, and without the need to roll them over. Perpetual futures are essentially an agreement between long and short counterparties. The short side needs to pay the long side some payoff based on the futures price at her entry and exit time, while the long side needs to pay the short side a flow intermediate cashflow termed as the funding rate. Different from traditional futures, perpetual futures have no expiration date. Both sides can enter the agreement at any time and profits and losses are marked to market continuously and credited to each side’s margin account. This setup improves the liquidity of the contract because there is no staggering of contracts with different maturities traded on the exchange and only a single perpetual futures contract per underlying is traded. Furthermore, this instrument does not require the market participants to deal with rolling over of their futures positions and is traded 24/7.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Unlike fixed-maturity futures, perpetuals are not guaranteed to converge to the spot price of their underlying asset at any time, and familiar no-arbitrage prices for perpetuals are not available.
To keep the gap between perpetual futures and spot prices small, long position holders periodically pay short position holders a “funding rate” proportional to this gap to incentivize trades that tend to narrow it.
For example, when the futures price substantially exceeds the spot price, arbitrageurs who borrow cash to long the spot and simultaneously short the futures would collect the funding rate. Their trades would tend to increase the spot price and decrease the futures price.
A narrow gap means that perpetual futures provide effective exposure to variation in the spot price of the underlying asset to hedging and speculating investors. Empirically, the funding rate is typically paid every eight hours with the value approximately equal to an average of futures-spot spread over the preceding eight hours.
Note that the strategy just sketched, commonly referred to as “funding rate arbitrage”, is not without risk even if one ignores margin requirements and trading costs, simply because there is no obvious maturity date at which the trade would be unwound at a profit.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">We derive no-arbitrage prices for perpetual futures in frictionless markets and derive no-arbitrage bounds for markets with trading costs.
The theoretical perpetual futures price is proportional to the spot price of the underlying, with a constant of proportionality that increases in the ratio of the interest rate to the funding rate. The interest rate captures the cost of borrowing cash to finance holding the underlying, while the funding rate captures the benefit of holding the futures.
Thus, intuitively, the future-spot spread is larger when the cash borrowing interest rate is large relative to the funding rate.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">Our derivation relies on a weaker notion of arbitrage that we call <em id="S1.p5.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">random-maturity arbitrage</em>. As its name suggests, unlike traditional riskless arbitrage, we allow the strategy’s time-to-maturity to be random. At first glance, one might object that such prices are not truly based on riskless arbitrage. Note, however, that riskless no-arbitrage pricing is usually just a useful fiction <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">Pedersen, 2019</a>)</cite>. For example, in real-world futures markets, arbitrageurs must maintain a margin account during the entire period in which the arbitrage trade is open. Temporary worsening of apparent arbitrage opportunities can lead to liquidations and losses. As the saying goes, the arbitrageur must remain liquid longer than the market stays irrational. Thus, even what theoretically appear to be riskless arbitrage opportunities may be quite risky.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p6.1" class="ltx_p">These no-arbitrage prices provide a useful benchmark for perpetual futures and simultaneously prescribe a strategy to exploit divergence from these fundamental values.
Motivated by the theoretical understanding, we study the empirical deviations of the perpetual futures price from the spot.
The mean absolute futures-spot spread is about 60% to 100% per year across different cryptocurrencies, which is considerably larger than the deviations documented in traditional currency markets by <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Du, Tepper, and Verdelhan (2018)</a></cite>.
We find strong comovement of the futures-spot gap across different cryptocurrencies. This comovement can be due to commonality in funding and market liquidity faced by arbitrageurs who operate in multiple cryptocurrencies. Common sentiment could also drive the difference in futures demand relative to the spot. Overall, the magnitude of the deviation is comparable to our theoretically calibrated no-arbitrage bound.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p7" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p7.1" class="ltx_p">The spread narrows considerably in 2022, suggesting a decrease in arbitrage frictions in the market and an increase in competition among arbitrageurs. The narrowing gap provides an additional perspective on the downfall of Alameda Research and Three Arrows Capital. According to news reports and interviews, both hedge funds seem to have pivoted from such arbitrage activity around late 2021 to early 2022 and started taking more directional bets on cryptocurrencies, with both direct unhedged crypto holdings and investments in crypto startups. The large declines in crypto prices in 2022 subsequently exhausted their capital and led to their bankruptcies.<span id="footnote1" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup>
            <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">1</span>
            
            
            
          See for example, Forbes, November 19, 2022, on <a href="https://www.forbes.com/sites/jeffkauflin/2022/11/19/how-did-sam-bankman-frieds-alameda-research-lose-so-much-money" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_href">How Did Sam Bankman-Fried’s Alameda Research Lose So Much Money?</a>, Odd Lots, November 17, 2022, on <a href="https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2022-11-17/odd-lots-podcast-understanding-sam-bankman-fried-s-ftx-crypto-collapse" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_href">Understanding the Collapse of Sam Bankman-Fried’s Crypto Empire</a>, and Hugh Hendry’s interview on December 3 2022 of Kyle Davies on the <a href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TzGdkB0xbCE" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_href">Collapse of Three Arrows Capital</a>.</span></span></span></p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p8" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p8.1" class="ltx_p">To understand the economics of the futures-spot spread, we first consider a trading strategy motivated by the random-maturity arbitrage theory. Whenever the futures-spot spread moves outside the theoretical bound under certain trading cost tiers, we open the trading position and close the position until the futures-spot spread returns to its theoretical relationship under no trading costs. We also consider a data-driven trading strategy with two trading thresholds. When the futures-spot spread is larger than the upper threshold, we enter the position to bet on the convergence of the two. We close the position when the futures-spot spread is smaller than the lower threshold. The threshold values are determined based on validation using historical data. We find that empirically, both trading strategies would deliver a sizable Sharpe ratio even under high trading costs. For example, for Bitcoin perpetual futures, both strategies generate Sharpe ratios ranging from 1.8 under high trading costs typical of retail investors who rarely trade, and up to 6.5 for highly-active market makers who pay no such fees.
The performance is even better for ETH and other cryptocurrencies.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p9" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p9.1" class="ltx_p">What explains these large no-arbitrage deviations?
One natural explanation is that liquidity in crypto markets is insufficient for arbitrageurs to eliminate such violations. Our finding that the spreads decline over time is consistent with liquidity improving as these markets develop, and leaves open the possibility that they will narrow going forward.
We also find, however, that past return momentum significantly explains the futures-spot gap with a time-series regression <math id="S1.p9.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>R</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R^{2}</annotation></semantics></math> of more than <math id="S1.p9.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="50\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>50</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">50\%</annotation></semantics></math>. When past returns are high, futures tend to be traded at a higher price relative to the spot. This indicates positive feedback or momentum trading behavior in the perpetual futures market. This correlation may linger even as crypto markets become more efficient.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p10" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p10.1" class="ltx_p">The existing literature on perpetual futures mainly focuses on providing some descriptive evidence. See e.g. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Alexander, Choi, Park, and
Sohn (2020)</a></cite>, <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Franz and Schmeling (2021)</a></cite>, <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">De Blasis and Webb (2022)</a></cite>, and <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ferko, Moin, Onur, and Penick (2022)</a></cite>. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Angeris, Chitra, Evans, and
Lorig (2022)</a></cite> provide a theoretical no-arbitrage analysis of the perpetual but they make over-simplifying assumptions by assuming the payoff from the perpetual will be a fixed function of the underlying spot price. Compared to the existing literature, we illustrate the fundamental mechanism behind the perpetual design and provide theoretical no-arbitrage price bound for this market.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p11" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p11.1" class="ltx_p">Also related is recent literature on fixed maturity futures in the crypto space. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">Schmeling, Schrimpf, and
Karamfil (2022)</a></cite> provides a comprehensive analysis of the carry of crypto futures, with the carry defined following the general definition of <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Koijen, Moskowitz, Pedersen, and
Vrugt (2018)</a></cite>. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">Schmeling, Schrimpf, and
Karamfil (2022)</a></cite> document a volatile convenience yield in the crypto space driven by high leverage from trend-chasing small investors and the relative scarcity of arbitrage capital. Our paper focuses on perpetual futures rather than fixed maturity futures and extends fixed maturity to random maturity no-arbitrage pricing.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p12" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p12.1" class="ltx_p">On the broader theme, our paper contributes to the understanding of the frictions and arbitrage in the cryptocurrency market. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">Makarov and Schoar (2020)</a></cite> study the price deviation across different exchanges. They find large gaps across countries, highlighting the important role played by capital control and slow-moving arbitrage capital as in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Duffie (2010)</a></cite>. Our analysis focuses on the price wedge between the spot and the futures market. We find that even within one exchange, there can be large deviations in the futures price from the theory-implied arbitrage-free value. The results indicate there are significant limits to arbitrage as in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gromb and Vayanos (2018)</a></cite> for cryptocurrencies in the early years.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p13" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p13.1" class="ltx_p">The rest of the paper is organized as follows: Section 2 provides the institutional details and history of perpetual futures. Section 3 presents the no-arbitrage analysis of the perpetual futures market and derives the theoretical price of perpetual futures. Section 4 demonstrates the empirical futures-spot deviation and presents the simple theory-motivated and data-driven trading strategy that can exploit the arbitrage opportunity. Section 5 provides some explanation for the deviation between futures and the spot. Section 6 concludes.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">2 </span>An Introduction to Perpetual Futures</h2>

<div id="S2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The idea of perpetual futures was first introduced in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">Shiller (1993)</a></cite>. The goal was to set up a perpetual claim on the cash flows of an illiquid asset. For example, the cash flow can be house rents and the underlying illiquid asset can be the real estate market. The purpose of the perpetual futures is to enable price discovery for the underlying with an illiquid or hard-to-measure price. Perpetual futures have no expiration date but cash flows will be exchanged between the long and the short side: after buying the perpetual futures, the long side will be entitled to receive the flow cash flow from the short side and they settle the price difference when exiting the position.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S2.F1" class="ltx_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1"><img src="2212.06888v2/figures/exchange_volume_v2.png" id="S2.F1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_figure_panel ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/181;" width="476" height="181" alt="Refer to caption"></div></div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 1: </span>Total trading volumes of perpetual futures across exchanges</figcaption><div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1">
<p id="S2.F1.2" class="ltx_p ltx_figure_panel">The figure displays the 7-day moving average daily traded volume for perpetual futures across all exchanges in blue. The median daily volume is $17.8 bn. (2020), $132.0 bn. (2021) and $101.9 bn. (2022). This translates to a yearly volume of $8,551 bn. (2020), $51,989 bn. (2021) and $39,306 bn. (2022) respectively. Additionally, the grey line depicts the ratio between the traded volume in perpetuals and spot markets. In 2022 the Perpetual markets are consistently trading between 2x or 3.5x the spot volume. The data is obtained from CoinGecko, a crypto data specialist. We exclude exchanges that are known for misrepresenting data (e.g. forms of wash trading).</p></div></div>
</figure>
<div id="S2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Perpetual futures in the crypto market have no expiration date and there will be cash flow exchange between the long and the short side but its purpose is different from Shiller’s original idea. Firstly, unlike, e.g. real estate market, crypto has no inherent dividend or cash flow. Secondly, the price discovery argument in Shiller’s idea is most applicable to settings where spot prices are difficult or impossible to measure. Crypto spot price can be measured from active tradings on different exchanges, and decentralized exchanges such as Bancor (<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hertzog et al. (2017)</a></cite>) or Uniswap (<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Adams et al. (2021)</a></cite>) can offer price discovery for assets with minimal liquidity. The major role perpetual futures play in the crypto space is to offer an effective leveraged trading vehicle to hedge or speculate the underlying spot price movement, which makes the market more complete. It also serves as an effective tax payment optimization tool for investors.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">The crypto perpetual futures were first introduced by BitMEX in 2016, which gained great popularity in the crypto space since its inception. Nowadays, based on data from CoinGecko, the median total daily trading volume of perpetual futures across all exchanges is 101.9 billion in the year 2022 which is about <math id="S2.p3.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="2\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2\times</annotation></semantics></math> to <math id="S2.p3.m2" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="3\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">3\times</annotation></semantics></math> the total spot trading volume across these exchanges. Figure <a href="#S2.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ 2 An Introduction to Perpetual Futures ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> presents the 7-day moving average of the total trading volume of perpetual futures across all exchanges. We see a significant rise in trading of perpetual futures around January 2021 and the total volume stabilizes at a level above $100 billion per day following the rise.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Cong, Li, Tang, and Yang (2022)</a></cite> document significant wash trading behavior among crypto exchanges because of competition, ranking mechanism, and lack of regulation. They find that over 70% of the trading volume on cryptos is not real. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Amiram, Lyandres, and
Rabetti (2020)</a></cite> confirmed this conclusion using new data and extended methodology. Therefore, in calculating the trading volume, we excluded exchanges that are known for misrepresenting data.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S2.F2" class="ltx_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1"><img src="2212.06888v2/figures/exchanges_fr_bitcoin.png" id="S2.F2.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_figure_panel ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/186;" width="476" height="186" alt="Refer to caption"></div></div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 2: </span>Bitcoin annualized funding rate across exchanges</figcaption><div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1">
<p id="S2.F2.2" class="ltx_p ltx_figure_panel">The figure presents the 7-day moving average annualized funding rate for Bitcoin (BTC) across exchanges. The data is obtained from glassnode, an analytics platform. The data covers two major market turbulences: the COVID stock market crash from February to April 2020, and the FTX insolvency in November 2022. The FTX collapse led to significant negative funding rates on all solvent exchanges, thus the perpetual future prices were lower than the spot prices on the solvent exchanges. Vice versa on the insolvent FTX. The funding rates become more volatile after the event, indicating increased uncertainty for the market participants.</p></div></div>
</figure>
<div id="S2.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p5.1" class="ltx_p">The key feature of crypto perpetual futures is the funding rate, which is the cash flow exchange between the long and the short side. Its goal is to keep the futures price close to the underlying spot so that the futures can be an effective hedging tool for underlying spot price movement. The funding rate is typically paid every 8 hours. The value would approximately equal a weighted average of the past 480 minutes’ price gap of the futures and the spot. If the futures price is above the spot, the funding rate will be positive, meaning the long side of the futures needs to pay the short side of the futures. This incentivizes traders to short the futures to bring the price back in line with the spot. On the other hand, when the futures price is below the spot, the short side needs to pay the long side the funding rate. Therefore, funding rate payment would be the key mechanism to keep the futures price close to the spot price.<span id="footnote2" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">2</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">2</sup>
            <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">2</span>
            
            
            
          <a href="https://www.binance.com/en/support/faq/360033525031" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">https://www.binance.com/en/support/faq/360033525031</a> provides a detailed explanation of how the funding rate is calculated.</span></span></span> It is worth noting that the perpetual futures are not equivalent to a rollover of 8-hour maturity futures. For the latter, every 8 hours, the price is guaranteed to converge to the underlying spot while for the perpetual futures, this is not the case.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p6.1" class="ltx_p">Figure <a href="#S2.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ 2 An Introduction to Perpetual Futures ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> presents the annualized 7-day moving average of BTC perpetual funding rate across different exchanges from January 2020 to December 2022. It covers the recent fallout of FTX. As can be seen, because of the active tradings in the perpetual market, the funding rate would reflect current market conditions. During the FTX episode and Covid market crash, we observe significant negative funding rates across solvent exchanges, suggesting pervasive market negative sentiment toward crypto as traders are willing to pay the funding rate to stay at the short side of the perpetual.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.p7" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p7.1" class="ltx_p">In the next part, we provide a theoretical characterization of the perpetual futures price and its relationship with the underlying spot price.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">3 </span>Risk-free Arbitrage in Perpetual Futures</h2>

<div id="S3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We provide a risk-free no-arbitrage analysis on the deviation of perpetual futures price from the spot in this section. Unlike traditional futures, perpetual futures have no expiration date. To analyze arbitrage in this market, we need to extend the traditional notion of risk-free arbitrage where arbitrageurs have a guaranteed positive payoff at a certain time in the future. We first describe the payoff structure of perpetual futures. Then we introduce the generalized notion of risk-free arbitrage with a guaranteed positive payoff at an uncertain time in the future.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Definition 1:</span> <span id="S3.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">A perpetual future <math id="S3.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\{F_{t}\}_{t=0}^{\infty}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msub><mi>F</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{F_{t}\}_{t=0}^{\infty}</annotation></semantics></math> written on <math id="S3.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\{S_{t}\}_{t=0}^{\infty}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{S_{t}\}_{t=0}^{\infty}</annotation></semantics></math> is an agreement between the long and the short side. There is <math id="S3.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0</annotation></semantics></math> cost to enter the agreement. After entering, both the long side and the short side can terminate the contract at any time <math id="S3.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math>. Before termination, for each unit of perpetual future, the long needs to pay the short a <math id="S3.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{F}_{s}-" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℱ</mi><mi>s</mi></msub><mo>−</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{F}_{s}-</annotation></semantics></math>adapted cash-flow <math id="S3.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\kappa(F_{s}-S_{s})ds,\,s\in(0,t)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi>κ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mi>s</mi></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>s</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow><mo rspace="0.337em">,</mo><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\kappa(F_{s}-S_{s})ds,\,s\in(0,t)</annotation></semantics></math>, referred to as the funding value. <math id="S3.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\kappa" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>κ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\kappa</annotation></semantics></math> is a scaling parameter determining the magnitude of the funding rate relative to the price gap. At termination, the short needs to pay the long <math id="S3.p2.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="F_{t}-F_{0}\," display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>F</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">F_{t}-F_{0}\,</annotation></semantics></math> for each unit shorted.</span></p>
</div>
<div id="S3.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p3.1" class="ltx_p">This definition is an approximation of real-world perpetual futures. In most exchanges, the funding value for perpetual futures is paid every <math id="S3.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="8" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>8</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">8</annotation></semantics></math> hours and approximately equals the difference between the futures price and the spot. If we measure time units in years, this setup would correspond to <math id="S3.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\kappa=1095" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>κ</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1095</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\kappa=1095</annotation></semantics></math>. Consider the case where the <math id="S3.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="F_{t}-S_{t}=C" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>C</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">F_{t}-S_{t}=C</annotation></semantics></math> over the 8-hour interval. The total funding rate payment over the 8 hours would be <math id="S3.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\frac{\kappa C}{3\times 365}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mfrac><mrow><mi>κ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>C</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mn>365</mn></mrow></mfrac><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{\kappa C}{3\times 365}</annotation></semantics></math>, which equals the price gap <math id="S3.p3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>C</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C</annotation></semantics></math> in the empirical setting. Therefore, we have <math id="S3.p3.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\kappa=1095" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>κ</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1095</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\kappa=1095</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p4.1" class="ltx_p">The traditional notions of arbitrage typically consider an uncertain payoff at a fixed future date.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p5.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Definition 2:</span> <span id="S3.p5.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">A traditional arbitrage opportunity is defined with respect to payoff <math id="S3.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>x</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math> at a certain future time <math id="S3.p5.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>T</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T</annotation></semantics></math> and its price <math id="S3.p5.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p(x)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p(x)</annotation></semantics></math>: if the following conditions are satisfied : (1) <math id="S3.p5.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x\geq 0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>≥</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x\geq 0</annotation></semantics></math> almost surely, (2) <math id="S3.p5.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x&gt;0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>&gt;</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x&gt;0</annotation></semantics></math> with some positive probability, (3) its price satisfies <math id="S3.p5.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p(x)\leq 0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>≤</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p(x)\leq 0</annotation></semantics></math>, then this payoff is an arbitrage opportunity (<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Cochrane (2009)</a></cite>).</span></p>
</div>
<div id="S3.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p6.1" class="ltx_p">There is no expiration date in the perpetual futures market. Therefore, a generalized notion of arbitrage would be required. Suppose the risk-free rate is constant, we consider <math id="S3.p6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0</annotation></semantics></math> costs strategies with a guaranteed positive payoff at an uncertain future time as a risk-free arbitrage. To state it formally:</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.p7" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p7.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.p7.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Definition 3:</span> <span id="S3.p7.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">A random-maturity arbitrage opportunity is defined with respect to a bounded random payoff <math id="S3.p7.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>x</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math> at a future random time <math id="S3.p7.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>τ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S3.p7.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau\in(0,\infty)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>τ</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau\in(0,\infty)</annotation></semantics></math>, and its price <math id="S3.p7.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p(x)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p(x)</annotation></semantics></math>: (1) <math id="S3.p7.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x\geq 0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>≥</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x\geq 0</annotation></semantics></math> almost surely, (2) <math id="S3.p7.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x&gt;0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>&gt;</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x&gt;0</annotation></semantics></math> with some positive probability, (3) its price satisfies <math id="S3.p7.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p(x)\leq 0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>≤</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p(x)\leq 0</annotation></semantics></math>, then this payoff is a random-maturity arbitrage opportunity.</span></p>
</div>
<div id="S3.p8" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p8.1" class="ltx_p">We restrict the payoff to be a bounded process to rule out doubling strategies as in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Dybvig and Huang (1988)</a></cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.p9" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p9.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.p9.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Corollary 1:</span> <span id="S3.p9.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">In the perpetual futures market, if a strategy (1) has <math id="S3.p9.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0</annotation></semantics></math> cost at time <math id="S3.p9.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0</annotation></semantics></math>, (2) for any price path of the futures and the spot, <math id="S3.p9.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\forall\{F_{t}\}_{t=0}^{\infty}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>∀</mo><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msub><mi>F</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></msubsup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\forall\{F_{t}\}_{t=0}^{\infty}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.p9.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\{S_{t}\}_{t=0}^{\infty}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{S_{t}\}_{t=0}^{\infty}</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S3.p9.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\exists\,t^{\prime}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo rspace="0.337em">∃</mo><msup><mi>t</mi><mo>′</mo></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\exists\,t^{\prime}</annotation></semantics></math> such that the discounted payoff of the strategy at time <math id="S3.p9.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t^{\prime}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>t</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t^{\prime}</annotation></semantics></math> is positive, then this strategy is a random-maturity arbitrage.</span></p>
</div>
<div id="S3.p10" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p10.1" class="ltx_p">This definition generalizes traditional arbitrage in the sense that there is a guaranteed positive payoff but at an uncertain future time. We next show that when there is no generalized risk-free arbitrage, the gap between futures and spot prices will be bounded by a constant. We make the two following assumptions:</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.p11" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p11.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.p11.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Assumption 1:</span> <span id="S3.p11.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">The gap between the perpetual futures and the spot is bounded by a constant <math id="S3.p11.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>M</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M</annotation></semantics></math>: <math id="S3.p11.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="|F_{t}-S_{t}|&lt;M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><mo>&lt;</mo><mi>M</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">|F_{t}-S_{t}|&lt;M</annotation></semantics></math>.</span></p>
</div>
<div id="S3.p12" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p12.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.p12.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Assumption 2:</span> <span id="S3.p12.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">The risk-free rate <math id="S3.p12.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>r</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r</annotation></semantics></math> for arbitrageurs is constant.</span></p>
</div>
<div id="S3.p13" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p13.1" class="ltx_p">Assumption 1 makes sure the price gap between the futures and the spot will follow a stationary path and assumption <math id="S3.p13.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>2</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2</annotation></semantics></math> guarantees that there is no roll-over risk for the arbitrageurs. With these two assumptions, we can state the conclusion as follows.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.p14" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p14.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.p14.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Proposition 1:</span> <span id="S3.p14.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Under assumptions <math id="S3.p14.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>1</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.p14.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>2</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2</annotation></semantics></math>, arbitrageurs in the market will trade the perpetual futures toward:</span></p>
<table id="S3.E1" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="F_{t}=S_{t}\left(1+\frac{r}{\kappa}\right)" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mi>r</mi><mi>κ</mi></mfrac></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">F_{t}=S_{t}\left(1+\frac{r}{\kappa}\right)</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(1)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
<div id="S3.2" class="ltx_proof">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_font_italic ltx_title_proof">Proof.</h6>
<div id="S3.p15" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p15.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.p15.1.1" class="ltx_text">To prove this proposition, we consider the following two scenarios in Table <a href="#S3.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ Proof. ‣ 3 Risk-free Arbitrage in Perpetual Futures ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>: (1) <math id="S3.p15.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="F_{0}&gt;S_{0}\left(1+\frac{r}{\kappa}\right)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>&gt;</mo><mrow><msub><mi>S</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mi>r</mi><mi>κ</mi></mfrac></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">F_{0}&gt;S_{0}\left(1+\frac{r}{\kappa}\right)</annotation></semantics></math>; (2) <math id="S3.p15.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="F_{0}&lt;S_{0}\left(1+\frac{r}{\kappa}\right)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>&lt;</mo><mrow><msub><mi>S</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mi>r</mi><mi>κ</mi></mfrac></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">F_{0}&lt;S_{0}\left(1+\frac{r}{\kappa}\right)</annotation></semantics></math>. We show in the first case, the arbitrageurs want to long the spot and short the futures because this is a random-maturity arbitrage opportunity and vice versa for the second case.</span></p>
</div>
<figure id="S3.T1" class="ltx_table">

<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 1: </span>Discounted Payoff to arbitrage strategies in perpetual futures and spot markets</figcaption><div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1">
<p id="S3.T1.3" class="ltx_p ltx_figure_panel">This table presents the costs and payoff two arbitrage trading strategies: (1) when <math id="S3.T1.m19" class="ltx_Math" alttext="F_{0}&gt;S_{0}\left(1+\frac{r}{\kappa}\right)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>&gt;</mo><mrow><msub><mi>S</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mi>r</mi><mi>κ</mi></mfrac></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">F_{0}&gt;S_{0}\left(1+\frac{r}{\kappa}\right)</annotation></semantics></math>, long the spot and short the futures; (2) when <math id="S3.T1.m20" class="ltx_Math" alttext="F_{0}&lt;S_{0}\left(1+\frac{r}{\kappa}\right)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>&lt;</mo><mrow><msub><mi>S</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mi>r</mi><mi>κ</mi></mfrac></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">F_{0}&lt;S_{0}\left(1+\frac{r}{\kappa}\right)</annotation></semantics></math>, long the futures and short the spot. In the last row, the payoff from exiting the position is the discounted payoff from future and spot price changes, proceeds from the cash market, and the funding rate.</p></div></div>
</figure>
<div id="S3.p16" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p16.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.p16.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Scenario 1:<span id="S3.p16.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium"> Firstly, if <math id="S3.p16.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="F_{0}&gt;S_{0}\left(1+\frac{r}{\kappa}\right)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>&gt;</mo><mrow><msub><mi>S</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mi>r</mi><mi>κ</mi></mfrac></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">F_{0}&gt;S_{0}\left(1+\frac{r}{\kappa}\right)</annotation></semantics></math>, consider the strategy of longing the spot and shorting the futures. We want to show that for any price path of the perpetual futures and the spot, there exists a future time <math id="S3.p16.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math> such that the strategy payoff is positive, i.e. this is a random-maturity arbitrage. Suppose not, then there exists price path <math id="S3.p16.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\{F_{t}\}_{t=0}^{\infty}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msub><mi>F</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{F_{t}\}_{t=0}^{\infty}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.p16.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\{S_{t}\}_{t=0}^{\infty}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{S_{t}\}_{t=0}^{\infty}</annotation></semantics></math> such that <math id="S3.p16.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\forall t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo rspace="0.167em">∀</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\forall t</annotation></semantics></math>, the discounted payoff from the strategy is negative:</span></span></p>
<table id="S3.Ex1" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.Ex1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="e^{-rt}F_{0}-e^{-rt}(F_{t}-S_{t})-S_{0}+\kappa\int_{0}^{t}(F_{s}-S_{s})e^{-rs}ds\leq 0" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mrow><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></mrow></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>F</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></mrow></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>S</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi>κ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><msubsup><mo rspace="0em">∫</mo><mn>0</mn><mi>t</mi></msubsup><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mi>s</mi></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>s</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow></mrow></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo rspace="0em">𝑑</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>≤</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">e^{-rt}F_{0}-e^{-rt}(F_{t}-S_{t})-S_{0}+\kappa\int_{0}^{t}(F_{s}-S_{s})e^{-rs}ds\leq 0</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.p16.2" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.p16.2.1" class="ltx_text">Denote <math id="S3.p16.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(F_{t}-S_{t})e^{-rt}\equiv u_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></mrow></msup></mrow><mo>≡</mo><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(F_{t}-S_{t})e^{-rt}\equiv u_{t}</annotation></semantics></math>, the inequality changes into:</span></p>
<table id="S3.Ex2" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.Ex2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="u_{t}\geq e^{-rt}F_{0}-S_{0}+\kappa\int_{0}^{t}u_{s}ds" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>≥</mo><mrow><mrow><mrow><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></mrow></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>F</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>S</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi>κ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><msubsup><mo>∫</mo><mn>0</mn><mi>t</mi></msubsup><mrow><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>s</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo rspace="0em">𝑑</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">u_{t}\geq e^{-rt}F_{0}-S_{0}+\kappa\int_{0}^{t}u_{s}ds</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.p16.3" class="ltx_p"><math id="S3.p16.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\underline{u}_{t}=e^{-rt}F_{0}-S_{0}+\kappa\int_{0}^{t}u_{s}ds" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><munder accentunder="true"><mi>u</mi><mo stretchy="true">¯</mo></munder><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mrow><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></mrow></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>F</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>S</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi>κ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><msubsup><mo>∫</mo><mn>0</mn><mi>t</mi></msubsup><mrow><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>s</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo rspace="0em">𝑑</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\underline{u}_{t}=e^{-rt}F_{0}-S_{0}+\kappa\int_{0}^{t}u_{s}ds</annotation></semantics></math><span id="S3.p16.3.1" class="ltx_text"> provides a lower bound for all processes <math id="S3.p16.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="u_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">u_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> satisfying the above inequality. Solving this integral equation, we have:</span></p>
<table id="S3.Ex3" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.Ex3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\underline{u}_{t}=\frac{F_{0}re^{-rt}}{\kappa+r}+\left(\frac{F_{0}}{1+\frac{r}{\kappa}}-S_{0}\right)e^{\kappa t}" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><munder accentunder="true"><mi>u</mi><mo stretchy="true">¯</mo></munder><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>r</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></mrow></msup></mrow><mrow><mi>κ</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>r</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>+</mo><mrow><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mfrac><msub><mi>F</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mi>r</mi><mi>κ</mi></mfrac></mrow></mfrac><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>S</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mi>κ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\underline{u}_{t}=\frac{F_{0}re^{-rt}}{\kappa+r}+\left(\frac{F_{0}}{1+\frac{r}{\kappa}}-S_{0}\right)e^{\kappa t}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.p16.4" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.p16.4.1" class="ltx_text">When <math id="S3.p16.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="F_{0}&gt;S_{0}\left(1+\frac{r}{\kappa}\right)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>&gt;</mo><mrow><msub><mi>S</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mi>r</mi><mi>κ</mi></mfrac></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">F_{0}&gt;S_{0}\left(1+\frac{r}{\kappa}\right)</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S3.p16.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lim_{t\rightarrow\infty}\underline{u}_{t}=\infty" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mo>lim</mo><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></mrow></msub><msub><munder accentunder="true"><mi>u</mi><mo stretchy="true">¯</mo></munder><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lim_{t\rightarrow\infty}\underline{u}_{t}=\infty</annotation></semantics></math>. This contradicts assumption 1, because it implies: <math id="S3.p16.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lim_{t\rightarrow\infty}(F_{t}-S_{t})e^{-rt}\geq\lim_{t\rightarrow\infty}\underline{u}_{t}\rightarrow\infty" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mo>lim</mo><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></mrow></msub><mrow><mrow><mo lspace="0em" stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></mrow></msup></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="0.1389em">≥</mo><mrow><msub><mo lspace="0.1389em" rspace="0.167em">lim</mo><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></mrow></msub><msub><munder accentunder="true"><mi>u</mi><mo stretchy="true">¯</mo></munder><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lim_{t\rightarrow\infty}(F_{t}-S_{t})e^{-rt}\geq\lim_{t\rightarrow\infty}\underline{u}_{t}\rightarrow\infty</annotation></semantics></math>. Therefore, when <math id="S3.p16.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="F_{0}&gt;S_{0}\left(1+\frac{r}{\kappa}\right)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>&gt;</mo><mrow><msub><mi>S</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mi>r</mi><mi>κ</mi></mfrac></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">F_{0}&gt;S_{0}\left(1+\frac{r}{\kappa}\right)</annotation></semantics></math>, longing the spot and shorting the futures would be a random-maturity arbitrage opportunity.</span></p>
</div>
<div id="S3.p17" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p17.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.p17.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Scenario 2:<span id="S3.p17.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium"> Next, if <math id="S3.p17.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="F_{0}&lt;S_{0}\left(1+\frac{r}{\kappa}\right)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>&lt;</mo><mrow><msub><mi>S</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mi>r</mi><mi>κ</mi></mfrac></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">F_{0}&lt;S_{0}\left(1+\frac{r}{\kappa}\right)</annotation></semantics></math>, consider the strategy of longing the futures and shorting the spot. Similarly, we want to show for this strategy, for any price path of the perpetual futures and the spot, there always exists a future time <math id="S3.p17.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math> such that the strategy payoff is positive, i.e. this is a random-maturity arbitrage. Suppose not, then there exists price path <math id="S3.p17.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\{F_{t}\}_{t=0}^{\infty}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msub><mi>F</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{F_{t}\}_{t=0}^{\infty}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.p17.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\{S_{t}\}_{t=0}^{\infty}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{S_{t}\}_{t=0}^{\infty}</annotation></semantics></math> such that <math id="S3.p17.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\forall t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo rspace="0.167em">∀</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\forall t</annotation></semantics></math>, the discounted payoff is negative:</span></span></p>
<table id="S3.Ex4" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.Ex4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="u_{t}\leq e^{-rt}F_{0}-S_{0}+\kappa\int_{0}^{t}u_{s}ds" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>≤</mo><mrow><mrow><mrow><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></mrow></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>F</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>S</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi>κ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><msubsup><mo>∫</mo><mn>0</mn><mi>t</mi></msubsup><mrow><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>s</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo rspace="0em">𝑑</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">u_{t}\leq e^{-rt}F_{0}-S_{0}+\kappa\int_{0}^{t}u_{s}ds</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.p17.2" class="ltx_p"><math id="S3.p17.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bar{u}_{t}=e^{-rt}F_{0}-S_{0}+\kappa\int_{0}^{t}u_{s}ds" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>u</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mrow><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></mrow></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>F</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>S</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi>κ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><msubsup><mo>∫</mo><mn>0</mn><mi>t</mi></msubsup><mrow><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>s</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo rspace="0em">𝑑</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bar{u}_{t}=e^{-rt}F_{0}-S_{0}+\kappa\int_{0}^{t}u_{s}ds</annotation></semantics></math><span id="S3.p17.2.1" class="ltx_text"> provides an upper bound for all processes <math id="S3.p17.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="u_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">u_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> satisfying the above inequality. This is the same integral equation as we see in the first case. We have:</span></p>
<table id="S3.Ex5" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">

</table>
<p id="S3.p17.3" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.p17.3.1" class="ltx_text">When <math id="S3.p17.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="F_{0}&lt;S_{0}\left(1+\frac{r}{\kappa}\right)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>&lt;</mo><mrow><msub><mi>S</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mi>r</mi><mi>κ</mi></mfrac></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">F_{0}&lt;S_{0}\left(1+\frac{r}{\kappa}\right)</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S3.p17.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lim_{t\rightarrow\infty}\bar{u}_{t}=-\infty" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mo>lim</mo><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></mrow></msub><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>u</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>−</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lim_{t\rightarrow\infty}\bar{u}_{t}=-\infty</annotation></semantics></math>. This contradicts assumption <math id="S3.p17.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>1</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1</annotation></semantics></math>, because <math id="S3.p17.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lim_{t\rightarrow\infty}(F_{t}-S_{t})e^{-rt}\leq\lim_{t\rightarrow\infty}\bar{u}_{t}\rightarrow-\infty" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mo>lim</mo><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></mrow></msub><mrow><mrow><mo lspace="0em" stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></mrow></msup></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="0.1389em">≤</mo><mrow><msub><mo lspace="0.1389em" rspace="0.167em">lim</mo><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></mrow></msub><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>u</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mrow><mo>−</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lim_{t\rightarrow\infty}(F_{t}-S_{t})e^{-rt}\leq\lim_{t\rightarrow\infty}\bar{u}_{t}\rightarrow-\infty</annotation></semantics></math>. Therefore, when <math id="S3.p17.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="F_{0}&lt;S_{0}\left(1+\frac{r}{\kappa}\right)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>&lt;</mo><mrow><msub><mi>S</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mi>r</mi><mi>κ</mi></mfrac></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">F_{0}&lt;S_{0}\left(1+\frac{r}{\kappa}\right)</annotation></semantics></math>, longing futures and shorting the spot would be a random-maturity arbitrage opportunity.
∎</span></p>
</div>
</div>
<div id="S3.p18" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p18.1" class="ltx_p">Proposition <math id="S3.p18.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>1</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1</annotation></semantics></math> states that when there are no frictions if there is a deviation of perpetual futures price from <math id="S3.p18.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S_{0}\left(1+\frac{r}{\kappa}\right)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>S</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mi>r</mi><mi>κ</mi></mfrac></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S_{0}\left(1+\frac{r}{\kappa}\right)</annotation></semantics></math>, arbitrageurs would have a strong incentive to trade because there would exist random-maturity arbitrage opportunities. The analysis can be easily extended to the case with constant trading costs (we may understand it as the bid-ask spread), where there would be a bound for the deviation between futures and spot price. Beyond such a bound, there would exist random-maturity arbitrage opportunities for the arbitrageurs. With this, we arrive at proposition 2:</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.p19" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p19.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.p19.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Proposition 2:</span> <span id="S3.p19.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">When there is a constant round-trip trading cost <math id="S3.p19.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>C</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C</annotation></semantics></math> the arbitrage trades in Table <a href="#S3.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ Proof. ‣ 3 Risk-free Arbitrage in Perpetual Futures ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>, arbitrageurs in the market will trade the perpetual futures until it lies within a bound of the spot:</span></p>
<table id="S3.Ex6" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.Ex6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S_{t}\left(1+\frac{r}{\kappa}\right)-C\leq F_{t}\leq S_{t}\left(1+\frac{r}{\kappa}\right)+C" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mi>r</mi><mi>κ</mi></mfrac></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mi>C</mi></mrow><mo>≤</mo><msub><mi>F</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>≤</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mi>r</mi><mi>κ</mi></mfrac></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>+</mo><mi>C</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S_{t}\left(1+\frac{r}{\kappa}\right)-C\leq F_{t}\leq S_{t}\left(1+\frac{r}{\kappa}\right)+C</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
<div id="S3.3" class="ltx_proof">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_font_italic ltx_title_proof">Proof.</h6>
<div id="S3.p20" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p20.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.p20.1.1" class="ltx_text">Using a similar argument as in proof to proposition 1. We can show that (1) when <math id="S3.p20.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="F_{0}\geq S_{0}(1+\frac{r}{\kappa})+C" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>≥</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>S</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mi>r</mi><mi>κ</mi></mfrac></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>+</mo><mi>C</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">F_{0}\geq S_{0}(1+\frac{r}{\kappa})+C</annotation></semantics></math>, longing the spot and shorting the futures would be a random-maturity arbitrage; (2) when <math id="S3.p20.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="F_{0}\leq S_{0}(1+\frac{r}{\kappa})-C" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>≤</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>S</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mi>r</mi><mi>κ</mi></mfrac></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mi>C</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">F_{0}\leq S_{0}(1+\frac{r}{\kappa})-C</annotation></semantics></math>, longing the futures and shorting the spot would be a random-maturity arbitrage. Therefore, whenever the price deviates away from the bound, the arbitrageurs would have a strong incentive to trade toward to bound.
∎</span></p>
</div>
</div>
<div id="S3.p21" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p21.1" class="ltx_p">In the presence of trading costs, when the deviation of perpetual futures price from <math id="S3.p21.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S_{0}(1+\frac{r}{k})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>S</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mi>r</mi><mi>k</mi></mfrac></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S_{0}(1+\frac{r}{k})</annotation></semantics></math>, is larger than the round-trip trading costs <math id="S3.p21.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>C</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C</annotation></semantics></math>, the arbitrageurs would have a strong incentive to trade perpetual futures toward the price <math id="S3.p21.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S_{0}(1+\frac{r}{\kappa})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>S</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mi>r</mi><mi>κ</mi></mfrac></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S_{0}(1+\frac{r}{\kappa})</annotation></semantics></math>. This proposition also prescribes a trading strategy to exploit the futures-spot divergence in markets with different levels of trading costs.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.p22" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p22.1" class="ltx_p">In the next part, we provide an empirical analysis of the futures-spot deviation and present arbitrage trading strategies motivated by our theory.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">4 </span>Data and Empirical Analysis</h2>

<div id="S4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We carry out an empirical analysis of the perpetual futures arbitrage trading strategies. In this part, we first describe the data. Next, we demonstrate empirically the deviation of the crypto futures-spot spread from the no-arbitrage benchmark. Following this, we implement two trading strategies that try to exploit the deviation. The first one is motivated by our theory of random-maturity arbitrage (random-maturity arbitrage strategy) and the second one is a pure data-driven where trading thresholds are determined based on data. (data-driven arbitrage strategy).</p>
</div>
<section id="S4.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.1 </span>Data</h3>

<div id="S4.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We focus on the 5 largest cryptocurrencies excluding the stablecoins: Bitcoin (BTC), Ether (ETH), BNB (BNB), Dogecoin (DOGE), and Cardano (ADA) with a total market cap of 529 billion, which account for 64.15% of the total market share of the Crypto market by November 2022.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">For each token, we obtain perpetual futures and spot prices at a 1-hour frequency from Binance. Binance is by far the leading exchange in the crypto realm. Another major benefit of using the Binance data is: nearly every part of our trading strategies can be completed within the same platform without delay in transferring the fund. So it reflects the real-time investment opportunities facing the traders.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">We also get the perpetual funding rate value from Binance. The funding rate is paid every 8 hours on Binance. So we have futures and spot prices every hour and realized funding rate payment at 8:00, 16:00, and 0:00 GMT each day. The perpetual and spot tradings are happening 24 hours per day and 7 days a week so there are no after-market hours in this market.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">We get the earliest possible data on perpetual futures trading from Binance. The table below lists the starting and ending dates of our data for each crypto. Our data ends on 2022-11-13, covering the latest fallout of the FTX.</p>
</div>
