<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 2: </span>Sample descriptions</figcaption><div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1">
<p id="S4.T2.3" class="ltx_p ltx_figure_panel">This table presents the sample start and end date for the 5 cryptocurrencies and their total number of observations.</p></div></div>
</figure>
<div id="S4.SS1.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">We obtain the trading costs from Binance’s website<span id="footnote3" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">3</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">3</sup>
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">3</span>
              
              
              
            <a href="https://www.binance.com/en/fee/trading" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">https://www.binance.com/en/fee/trading</a> provides data on trading fees in perpetual futures and the spot market</span></span></span>. In general, the trading costs for the spot market are significantly larger than that for the perpetual futures for similar trading volume because futures typically are traded with leverage. Fee tiers are attributed to the 30-day trading volume. We attribute high trading costs with a 30-day spot trading volume above $1 million and futures trading volume above $15 million (small individual trader). Medium trading costs attribute to a 30-day spot trading volume above $150 million and futures trading volume above $1 billion (small funds). Low trading costs attribute to a 30-day spot trading volume above $2 billion and futures trading volume above 12.5 billion (large funds). No fee can be negotiated with customized contracts, for example for market makers. We consider trading costs for makers instead of takers because institutions typically trade maker orders.<span id="footnote4" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">4</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">4</sup>
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">4</span>
              
              
              
            Takers trade market orders while makers trade limit orders. Takers take liquidity from the market while makers make the market or provide liquidity to the market.</span></span></span> Table <a href="#S4.T3" title="Table 3 ‣ 4.1 Data ‣ 4 Data and Empirical Analysis ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> presents the specification of different trading costs. It also shows the random-maturity arbitrage bound for the deviation between the perpetual futures and the no-arbitrage price (<math id="S4.SS1.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho_{l}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>ρ</mi><mi>l</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho_{l}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S4.SS1.p5.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho_{u}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>ρ</mi><mi>u</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho_{u}</annotation></semantics></math>). The bounds become wider as the trading costs increase. Detailed explanations of the trading costs specifications are also provided in appendix Figure <a href="#Sx1.F8" title="Figure 8 ‣ A. Additional figures and tables ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">8</span></a> and Figure <a href="#Sx1.F9" title="Figure 9 ‣ A. Additional figures and tables ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">9</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p6.1" class="ltx_p">To measure the deviation from the no-arbitrage price, we also obtain the interest rate data from Aave, a leading open-source DeFi liquidity protocol. Customers on Aave can either be a supplier or a borrower of cryptocurrencies. Because of the anonymity and decentralization of DeFi system, all borrowings are over-collateralized and the collateral can serve as an additional supply to the system for borrowing. The customers can also supply spare currencies to the system to earn an interest rate. The supply interest rate is typically different from the borrowing interest rate. Both interest rates and their wedge are determined algorithmically based on the market condition of supply and demand. We use interest rates from this platform because we believe it is a good proxy for the funding condition in the crypto market. Our results are robust if we use the interest rate from the traditional financial market.<span id="footnote5" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">5</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">5</sup>
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">5</span>
              
              
              
            We also run our analysis using daily T-bill rates obtained from Kenneth French’s website at <a href="https://mba.tuck.dartmouth.edu/pages/faculty/ken.french/Data_Library/f-f_factors.html" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">https://mba.tuck.dartmouth.edu/pages/faculty/ken.french/Data_Library/f-f_factors.html</a>. The results are very close to ones using crypto market supply and borrowing rates.</span></span></span></p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p7" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p7.1" class="ltx_p">Our theory indicates using a risk-free rate available to the arbitrageurs. Therefore, we consider the interest rates on the stablecoins, which are not subject to volatile spot price movement and are the currency of denomination for perpetual futures margins. There are three major stablecoins traded on Aave: USDT, USDC, and DAI. To get a robust measure of the risk-free rate, we take an average of the three interest rates to arrive at our final risk-free supply and borrowing rate for the arbitrageurs.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p8" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p8.1" class="ltx_p">We plot the time-series evolvement of the interest rate in the appendix Figure <a href="#Sx1.F11" title="Figure 11 ‣ A. Additional figures and tables ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">11</span></a>. During the early years, we see higher interest rate volatility due to the funding liquidity of the DeFi platform. In later samples, interest rates are more stable and approach interest rates in traditional financial markets.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p9" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p9.1" class="ltx_p">Our interest rate data starts from 2020-01-08. Therefore, for coins with perpetual data available before the time (BTC and ETH), we begin the analysis from 2020-01-08. For other coins (BNB, DOGE, ADA), we begin the analysis from the time when they have data available.</p>
</div>

<div class="ltx_flex_figure ltx_flex_table">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1">

</thead>
<tbody class="ltx_tbody">
<tr id="S4.T3.2.2" class="ltx_tr">
<th id="S4.T3.2.2.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_th ltx_th_row ltx_border_t">No</th>
<td id="S4.T3.2.2.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_border_t">
<span id="S4.T3.2.2.2.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top">
<span id="S4.T3.2.2.2.1.1" class="ltx_p ltx_align_center">0%</span>
</span></td>
<td id="S4.T3.2.2.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_border_t">
<span id="S4.T3.2.2.3.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top">
<span id="S4.T3.2.2.3.1.1" class="ltx_p ltx_align_center">0%</span>
</span></td>
<td id="S4.T3.2.2.4" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_border_t">
<span id="S4.T3.2.2.4.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top">

</table></div></div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 3: </span>Trading costs specifications</figcaption><div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1">
<p id="S4.T3.3" class="ltx_p ltx_figure_panel">This table reports our specification of 4 different levels of trading costs: no, low, medium, and high. Fee tiers are attributed to the 30-day trading volume. We attribute high fees with a 30-day trading volume above $1mn in spot and above $15mn in perpetual, typically an individual trader. Medium fees attribute to a 30-day trading volume above $150mn in spot and above $1bn in perpetual (small funds). Low fees attribute to a 30-day trading volume above $2bn in spot and above $12.5bn in perpetual (large funds). No fees can be negotiated with customized contracts, for example for market makers. We also report the theory implied no arbitrage bound (<math id="S4.T3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho_{l}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>ρ</mi><mi>l</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho_{l}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S4.T3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho_{u}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>ρ</mi><mi>u</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho_{u}</annotation></semantics></math>) for <math id="S4.T3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ρ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho</annotation></semantics></math> under different trading costs specifications. They are calculated using the following formulas: <math id="S4.T3.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho_{l}=\kappa log\left(1-C\right)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>ρ</mi><mi>l</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>κ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>l</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>o</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>g</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mi>C</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho_{l}=\kappa log\left(1-C\right)</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S4.T3.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho_{u}=\kappa log\left(1+C\right)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>ρ</mi><mi>u</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>κ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>l</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>o</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>g</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mi>C</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho_{u}=\kappa log\left(1+C\right)</annotation></semantics></math>, where <math id="S4.T3.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>C</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C</annotation></semantics></math> is the round-trip percentage trading costs of the long-short strategy of perpetual and spot.</p></div></div>
</figure>
<div id="S4.SS1.p10" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p10.1" class="ltx_p">To explain the deviation between perpetual futures and the spot, we also get the data of fear and greed index from alternative.me.<span id="footnote6" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">6</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">6</sup>
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">6</span>
              
              
              
            <a href="https://alternative.me/crypto/fear-and-greed-index/" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">https://alternative.me/crypto/fear-and-greed-index/</a> provides the data on the fear and greed index</span></span></span> This index ranges from 0 to 100 and is constructed using past market return momentum, volatility, social media sentiment, the concentration of crypto market share, and google trends.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.2 </span>Deviations of perpetual futures from no-arbitrage benchmarks</h3>

<div id="S4.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">If we define the annualized deviation <math id="S4.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ρ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho</annotation></semantics></math> as the interest rate that rationalizes an observed future-spot spread, then:</p>
<table id="S4.Ex7" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S4.Ex7.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="F=S\left(1+\frac{r+\rho}{\kappa}\right)" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>F</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>S</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>ρ</mi></mrow><mi>κ</mi></mfrac></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">F=S\left(1+\frac{r+\rho}{\kappa}\right)</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S4.SS2.p1.2" class="ltx_p">Use <math id="S4.SS2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>f</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S4.SS2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>s</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s</annotation></semantics></math> to denote <math id="S4.SS2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="log(F)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>o</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>g</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>F</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">log(F)</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S4.SS2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="log(S)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>o</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>g</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>S</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">log(S)</annotation></semantics></math> respectively. We can obtain the following approximate equation for <math id="S4.SS2.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ρ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho</annotation></semantics></math>:</p>
<table id="S4.E2" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S4.E2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho\approx\kappa(f-s)-r" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ρ</mi><mo>≈</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>κ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mi>r</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho\approx\kappa(f-s)-r</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(2)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S4.SS2.p1.3" class="ltx_p">This definition is the same in spirit to <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Du et al. (2018)</a></cite> who define the CIP deviation as the wedge that would equate the dollar borrowing rate and the synthetic dollar borrowing rate. <math id="S4.SS2.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ρ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho</annotation></semantics></math> is the fundamental object we focus on in our empirical research.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">At each hour, we calculate <math id="S4.SS2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ρ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho</annotation></semantics></math> using data on perpetual futures price, spot price, and the crypto risk-free interest rate. When the perpetual futures price is above the spot, the arbitrageurs need to short the futures and long the spot. She needs to finance her position by borrowing from the cash market (as is shown in Table <a href="#S3.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ Proof. ‣ 3 Risk-free Arbitrage in Perpetual Futures ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>). Therefore, we use the borrowing rate from Aave as the risk-free rate. On the other hand, when the perpetual futures price is below the spot, the arbitrageurs need to short the futures and long the spot. She may invest the proceed from shorting in the cash market (as is shown in Table <a href="#S3.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ Proof. ‣ 3 Risk-free Arbitrage in Perpetual Futures ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>). Therefore, we use the supply rate from Aave as the risk-free rate.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.F3" class="ltx_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1">
<div id="S4.F3.2" class="ltx_logical-block ltx_figure_panel">
          
<div id="S4.F3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent ltx_align_center"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2212.06888v2/fig1.svg" id="S4.F3.p1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/234;" width="476" height="234"></object>
</div>
        
</div></div></div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 3: </span>Deviations of perpetual futures from no-arbitrage benchmarks</figcaption><div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1">
<p id="S4.F3.3" class="ltx_p ltx_figure_panel">This figure presents the 7-day moving averages of the annualized deviation of the perpetual futures-spot spread from the no-arbitrage benchmark for the five cryptocurrencies. The deviation <math id="S4.F3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ρ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho</annotation></semantics></math> is defined as <math id="S4.F3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho=\kappa(f-s)-r" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ρ</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>κ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mi>r</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho=\kappa(f-s)-r</annotation></semantics></math>.</p></div></div>
</figure>
<figure id="S4.F4" class="ltx_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1"><img src="2212.06888v2/fig3.png" id="S4.F4.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_figure_panel ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/280;" width="476" height="280" alt="Refer to caption"></div></div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 4: </span>Correlation of <math id="S4.F4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ρ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho</annotation></semantics></math>, funding rate, spot returns and fear &amp; greed index</figcaption><div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1">
<p id="S4.F4.2" class="ltx_p ltx_figure_panel">This figure presents the correlation among different crypto’s futures-spot deviation <math id="S4.F4.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ρ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho</annotation></semantics></math> (row 1 to 5), funding rate (row 6 to 10), fear &amp; greed index (row 11) and the spot returns (row 12-16).</p></div></div>
</figure>
<div id="S4.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Figure <a href="#S4.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ 4.2 Deviations of perpetual futures from no-arbitrage benchmarks ‣ 4 Data and Empirical Analysis ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> presents the 7-day moving average of <math id="S4.SS2.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ρ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho</annotation></semantics></math> for each of the five cryptocurrencies. There is significant comovement in futures spot spread across all five cryptocurrencies, suggesting there exists a common factor driving the wedge. Figure <a href="#S4.F4" title="Figure 4 ‣ 4.2 Deviations of perpetual futures from no-arbitrage benchmarks ‣ 4 Data and Empirical Analysis ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a> confirms this finding: the futures spot deviations covary with each other. By design, they also highly correlate with funding rate. The funding rate does not correlate perfectly with the average futures spot gap because: in real implementations, (1) there is a clamp region, within which the funding rate equals 0.01%; (2) the funding rate is calculated as a weighted average of perpetual spot price deviation, with larger weight being put on more recent observations; (3) in calculating the funding rate, Binance does not just consider the quote price, they also use an impact margin notional to consider price impact of the trade.<span id="footnote7" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">7</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">7</sup>
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">7</span>
              
              
              
            The details of the funding rate calculation can be found at: <a href="https://www.binance.com/en/support/faq/360033525031" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">https://www.binance.com/en/support/faq/360033525031</a>.</span></span></span></p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Moreover, a fear and greed index can significantly explain the common comovement. The correlation of futures-spot deviation with the spot market return is low. The spot returns are highly correlated across different cryptos, consistent with the strong common market factor results from <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al. (2022)</a></cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p5.1" class="ltx_p">From our theoretical analysis, the arbitrageurs will only accommodate the demand in the market if the price deviation is larger than the trading costs. So the overall sentiment in the futures market relative to the spot will manifest itself in the price gap between the futures and spot. If the sentiment in the different markets is driven by a common factor, then we expect to find a high comovement for the futures spot spread. In part 5, we provide further analysis to explain the futures spot spread. We find that past returns of each crypto are significant explanatory variables for the time-series variation in the spread. This can also easily explain the low correlation of the future spot spreads with spot returns: the deviation represents a persistent component of sentiment that does not comove with volatile spot price movement.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p6.1" class="ltx_p">Furthermore, we find that after the year 2022, the futures spot spreads become smaller in magnitude and less volatile compared to the earlier years. The 7-day moving average stays within -100% and 0% most of the time for the 5 cryptocurrencies while larger sways in earlier years are quite common. This suggests the market is becoming increasingly efficient.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.3 </span>Random-maturity Arbitrage Strategy</h3>

<div id="S4.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this part, we provide a trading strategy motivated by our random-maturity arbitrage theory. Table <a href="#S4.T3" title="Table 3 ‣ 4.1 Data ‣ 4 Data and Empirical Analysis ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> presents under different trading costs, the bounds (<math id="S4.SS3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho_{l}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>ρ</mi><mi>l</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho_{l}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S4.SS3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho_{u}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>ρ</mi><mi>u</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho_{u}</annotation></semantics></math>) beyond which there exist random-maturity arbitrage opportunities. We consider a simple trading strategy, whenever the <math id="S4.SS3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ρ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho</annotation></semantics></math> enters the region outside the annualized round-trip trading costs in Table <a href="#S4.T3" title="Table 3 ‣ 4.1 Data ‣ 4 Data and Empirical Analysis ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>, we open the position. We close the position until the <math id="S4.SS3.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ρ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho</annotation></semantics></math> first goes back to 0.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.F5" class="ltx_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1"><img src="2212.06888v2/figure_trading_theory_BTC.png" id="S4.F5.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_figure_panel ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/239;" width="476" height="239" alt="Refer to caption"></div></div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 5: </span>Random-maturity Arbitrage Strategy: Bitcoin, high trading costs</figcaption><div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1">
<p id="S4.F5.2" class="ltx_p ltx_figure_panel">This figure presents the futures/spot deviation and trading thresholds of the random-maturity arbitrage strategy we implement for BTC under high trading costs. Each blue dot in the figure represents annualized deviation of futures from the spot <math id="S4.F5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho=\kappa(f-s)-r" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ρ</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>κ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mi>r</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho=\kappa(f-s)-r</annotation></semantics></math>. The orange line is the open-position threshold and the red line is the close-position threshold.</p></div></div>
</figure>
<div id="S4.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Figure <a href="#S4.F5" title="Figure 5 ‣ 4.3 Random-maturity Arbitrage Strategy ‣ 4 Data and Empirical Analysis ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a> provides an illustration of the trading strategy. When the deviation is beyond the orange lines, the strategy would open a trading position. The position will be closed at the time when the futures/spot deviation first hits the red line. We present trading thresholds across different trading costs for different currencies in Figure <a href="#Sx1.F12" title="Figure 12 ‣ A. Additional figures and tables ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">12</span></a> in the appendix. Different trading strategies have the same close-position line which is equal to the risk-free rate while the open-position line adjusts to the level of trading costs.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Since our trading strategy is a thresholding trading rule, we follow <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lucca and Moench (2015)</a></cite> to make adjustments to the Sharpe ratio. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lucca and Moench (2015)</a></cite> consider a trading strategy that is only active on FOMC announcement dates. Relating this to our context, we first calculate the mean (<math id="S4.SS3.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mu" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>μ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mu</annotation></semantics></math>) and standard deviation (<math id="S4.SS3.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>σ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma</annotation></semantics></math>) of our trading strategy during the time it is active. Next, we scale the <math id="S4.SS3.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mu/\sigma" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>μ</mi><mo>/</mo><mi>σ</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mu/\sigma</annotation></semantics></math> by the number of the period the strategy is active in a year:</p>
<table id="S4.Ex8" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S4.Ex8.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="SR=\frac{\mu}{\sigma}\sqrt{N_{a}}" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>S</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>R</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mfrac><mi>μ</mi><mi>σ</mi></mfrac><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msqrt><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>a</mi></msub></msqrt></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">SR=\frac{\mu}{\sigma}\sqrt{N_{a}}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S4.SS3.p3.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S4.SS3.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mu" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>μ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mu</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S4.SS3.p3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>σ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma</annotation></semantics></math> are average hourly returns and <math id="S4.SS3.p3.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N_{a}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>a</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N_{a}</annotation></semantics></math> is the average number of hours the strategy is active in a year. We follow the same approach to annualize the returns and standard deviations: <math id="S4.SS3.p3.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mu_{ann}=\mu N_{a}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>μ</mi><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>n</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>μ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>a</mi></msub></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mu_{ann}=\mu N_{a}</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S4.SS3.p3.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma_{ann}=\sigma\sqrt{N_{a}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>σ</mi><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>n</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>σ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msqrt><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>a</mi></msub></msqrt></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma_{ann}=\sigma\sqrt{N_{a}}</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>

<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 4: </span>Performance of Random-maturity Arbitrage Trading Strategy: High Trading Cost</figcaption><div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1">
<p id="S4.T4.3" class="ltx_p ltx_figure_panel">This table presents the annual return, standard deviations, and Sharpe ratios of the random-maturity arbitrage trading strategies for the 5 different cryptocurrencies with high trading costs. We also report the proportion of time the trading strategy has an open position. We break down returns into each year and also provide summary stat across all time. The left panel shows the performance of the unrestricted trading strategy where both long and short spot is allowed. The right panel shows the performance of the long-spot-only trading strategy where shorting the spot is not allowed.</p></div></div>
</figure>
<div id="S4.SS3.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Table <a href="#S4.T4" title="Table 4 ‣ 4.3 Random-maturity Arbitrage Strategy ‣ 4 Data and Empirical Analysis ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a> presents the trading performance of the strategy under high trading costs. We consider two cases: (1) unrestricted; (2) long-spot only. We consider the second case because, in earlier years of crypto, the infrastructure of shorting the crypto is not well-established. As is implied by our theory, whenever the deviation between futures and spot is larger than the trading costs, performing a random-maturity arbitrage strategy would generate returns with high SR. After trading costs, the strategy can generate a SR of 1.77 for BTC and much higher SRs for other Cryptos.</p>
</div>

<span id="S4.T5.2.21.5.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top">
<span id="S4.T5.2.21.5.1.1" class="ltx_p ltx_align_center">5.59</span>
</span></td>
<td id="S4.T5.2.21.6" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left">
<span id="S4.T5.2.21.6.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top">
<span id="S4.T5.2.21.6.1.1" class="ltx_p ltx_align_center">5.17</span>
</span></td></tr>
<tr id="S4.T5.2.22" class="ltx_tr">
<th id="S4.T5.2.22.1" class="ltx_td ltx_th ltx_th_row ltx_border_bb"></th>
<th id="S4.T5.2.22.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_th ltx_th_row ltx_border_bb">SR</th>
<td id="S4.T5.2.22.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_border_bb">
<span id="S4.T5.2.22.3.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top">
<span id="S4.T5.2.22.3.1.1" class="ltx_p ltx_align_center">10.20</span>
</span></td>
<td id="S4.T5.2.22.4" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_border_bb">
<span id="S4.T5.2.22.4.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top">
<span id="S4.T5.2.22.4.1.1" class="ltx_p ltx_align_center">5.74</span>
</span></td>
<td id="S4.T5.2.22.5" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_border_bb">

<span id="S4.T5.2.22.5.1.1" class="ltx_p ltx_align_center">3.70</span>
</span></td>
<td id="S4.T5.2.22.6" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_border_bb">
<span id="S4.T5.2.22.6.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top">
<span id="S4.T5.2.22.6.1.1" class="ltx_p ltx_align_center">2.97</span>
</span></td></tr>
</tbody>
</table></div></div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 5: </span>Performance of Random-maturity Arbitrage Strategy under Different Trading Costs</figcaption><div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1">
<p id="S4.T5.3" class="ltx_p ltx_figure_panel">This table presents the portfolio performance under different trading cost specifications. The fees for spots are 2.25 bps, 4.5 bps, and 6.75 bps for the low, medium, and high trading cost levels. The fees for the futures are 0.18 bp, 0.72 bp, and 1.44 bps for low, medium, and high trading cost levels.</p></div></div>
</figure>
<div id="S4.SS3.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p5.1" class="ltx_p">As time goes by, the perpetual futures market seems to become more and more efficient. As we can see in 2022, the deviation of crypto price from the arbitrage-free bound is much less frequent compared to earlier years. But when the deviation happens, the resulting SR from the trade is still very high.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p6.1" class="ltx_p">Table <a href="#S4.T5" title="Table 5 ‣ 4.3 Random-maturity Arbitrage Strategy ‣ 4 Data and Empirical Analysis ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a> presents the strategy’s performance under different trading costs. As trading costs decrease, the random-maturity arbitrage strategy takes more active trades and the SRs of the strategy also increase.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.p7" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p7.1" class="ltx_p">The success of the trading strategy supports the theory of random-maturity arbitrage. Whenever there is a deviation larger than the gap implied by the theory, betting on the convergence would generate a positive payoff at some uncertain future time. Therefore, the convergence arbitrage trade would generate high SR.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.4 </span>Data-driven Futures-spot Arbitrage Strategy</h3>

<div id="S4.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In the previous section, we demonstrate the profitability of a simple theory-motivated trading strategy. The trading threshold can also be potentially further improved using a data-driven way. In this part, we implement a data-driven two-threshold arbitrage trading strategy in the perpetual futures market. The strategy can be characterized with a tuple of two thresholds: <math id="S4.SS4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(u,l)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>u</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(u,l)</annotation></semantics></math>, where <math id="S4.SS4.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="u" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>u</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">u</annotation></semantics></math> denotes the upper bar and <math id="S4.SS4.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="l" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>l</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">l</annotation></semantics></math> denotes the lower bar, <math id="S4.SS4.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="u&gt;l" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>u</mi><mo>&gt;</mo><mi>l</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">u&gt;l</annotation></semantics></math>. When <math id="S4.SS4.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho&gt;u" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ρ</mi><mo>&gt;</mo><mi>u</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho&gt;u</annotation></semantics></math>, we long the spot and short the futures. When <math id="S4.SS4.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="-l&lt;\rho&lt;l" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo><mi>l</mi></mrow><mo>&lt;</mo><mi>ρ</mi><mo>&lt;</mo><mi>l</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">-l&lt;\rho&lt;l</annotation></semantics></math>, we close the existing position. When <math id="S4.SS4.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho&lt;-u" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ρ</mi><mo>&lt;</mo><mrow><mo>−</mo><mi>u</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho&lt;-u</annotation></semantics></math>, we long the futures and short the spot. Figure <a href="#S4.F6" title="Figure 6 ‣ 4.4 Data-driven Futures-spot Arbitrage Strategy ‣ 4 Data and Empirical Analysis ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a> presents an illustration of the strategy for Bitcoin with the trading thresholds estimated using real-time data.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.F6" class="ltx_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1"><img src="2212.06888v2/figure_trading_4_btc.png" id="S4.F6.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_figure_panel ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/239;" width="476" height="239" alt="Refer to caption"></div></div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 6: </span>Two-threshold trading strategy: Bitcoin, high trading costs</figcaption><div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1">
<p id="S4.F6.2" class="ltx_p ltx_figure_panel">This figure presents real-time trading thresholds of the arbitrage strategy we implement for BTC under high trading costs. Each blue dot in the figure represents annualized deviation of futures from the spot <math id="S4.F6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho=\kappa(f-s)-r" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ρ</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>κ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mi>r</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho=\kappa(f-s)-r</annotation></semantics></math>. The orange line is the open-position threshold and the red line is the close-position threshold.</p></div></div>
</figure>
<div id="S4.SS4.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS4.p2.1" class="ltx_p">To determine the optimal <math id="S4.SS4.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(u,l)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>u</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(u,l)</annotation></semantics></math>, at the beginning of each month, we calculate the returns of the two-threshold trading strategy based on the past 6 months’ data on a grid of parameters. From Table <a href="#S4.T3" title="Table 3 ‣ 4.1 Data ‣ 4 Data and Empirical Analysis ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>, we find the theory implied bounds for price deviation across all trading costs specifications lie within <math id="S4.SS4.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="-200\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mn>200</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">-200\%</annotation></semantics></math> to <math id="S4.SS4.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="+200\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mn>200</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">+200\%</annotation></semantics></math>. So we choose the grid as increasing from <math id="S4.SS4.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0\%</annotation></semantics></math> to <math id="S4.SS4.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="200\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>200</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">200\%</annotation></semantics></math> with an incremental step of <math id="S4.SS4.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="10\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>10</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">10\%</annotation></semantics></math> for <math id="S4.SS4.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="u" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>u</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">u</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S4.SS4.p2.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="l" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>l</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">l</annotation></semantics></math> (<math id="S4.SS4.p2.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="u\geq l" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>u</mi><mo>≥</mo><mi>l</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">u\geq l</annotation></semantics></math>). In total, there are <math id="S4.SS4.p2.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="210" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>210</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">210</annotation></semantics></math> model specifications. We choose the model that delivers the highest Sharpe Ratio in the validation sample of the past 6 months.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS4.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS4.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Figure <a href="#S4.F6" title="Figure 6 ‣ 4.4 Data-driven Futures-spot Arbitrage Strategy ‣ 4 Data and Empirical Analysis ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a> presents the real-time trading thresholds of our arbitrage strategy for BTC under high trading costs. To mitigate the trading cost, the strategy automatically chooses a much lower close-position threshold compared to the open-position threshold. We also present the visualization of all trading strategies under different trading costs in appendix Figure <a href="#Sx1.F13" title="Figure 13 ‣ A. Additional figures and tables ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">13</span></a> to <a href="#Sx1.F16" title="Figure 16 ‣ A. Additional figures and tables ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">16</span></a>. Under no-trading costs, the strategy chooses a low open-position threshold and the open- and close-position thresholds coincide with each other. Since there is no trading cost, the strategy no longer needs to wait for price convergence to avoid high turnover. On the contrary, with high trading costs, the strategy chooses a larger open-position threshold and a smaller close-position threshold. This reflects the automatic adjustment from the algorithm for trading costs and turnovers.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS4.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS4.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Table <a href="#S4.T6" title="Table 6 ‣ 4.4 Data-driven Futures-spot Arbitrage Strategy ‣ 4 Data and Empirical Analysis ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a> presents the return statistics for this strategy under high trading costs over time. In the baseline ‘unrestricted’ strategy, we allow for both (1) longing the futures and shorting the spot and (2) shorting the futures and longing the spot while in the ‘long-spot only’ strategy, we only allow for shorting the futures and longing the spot. The reason we consider the ‘long-spot only’ strategy is the infrastructure for shorting the spot is not well-developed. So we want to examine the performance of the trading strategy in the presence of such limits to arbitrage.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.T6" class="ltx_table">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure ltx_flex_table">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1">

</table></div></div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 6: </span>Portfolio Performance: High Trading Cost</figcaption><div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1">
<p id="S4.T6.3" class="ltx_p ltx_figure_panel">This table presents the annual return, standard deviations, Sharpe ratios of the two-threshold trading strategies for the 5 different cryptocurrencies with high trading costs. We also report the proportion of time the trading strategy has an open position. We break down returns into each year and also provide summary stat across all time. The left panel shows the performance of the unrestricted trading strategy where both long and short spot is allowed. The right panel shows the performance of the long-spot-only trading strategy where shorting the spot is not allowed.</p></div></div>
</figure>
<div id="S4.SS4.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS4.p5.1" class="ltx_p">We find the arbitrage trading strategy has a high Sharpe ratio under high trading costs. The annualized Sharpe ratio for Bitcoin is 1.78 in our sample. They are even higher for other cryptos. The high Sharpe ratio of the trading strategy corroborates our theoretical results that when the price deviation is large enough, the trading would be a random-maturity arbitrage opportunity.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS4.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS4.p6.1" class="ltx_p">In the year 2022, the deviation between the futures and the spot becomes smaller and less volatile. There seems to be a structural break. We indeed find the trading strategy takes less active positions and significantly lower annualized returns. However, when there is a large enough deviation, the strategy can still generate sizeable Sharpe ratios in trading.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS4.p7" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS4.p7.1" class="ltx_p">The conclusion and results remain similar if we consider ‘long-spot only’ trading strategies where only shorting the futures and longing the spot is allowed. Considering this one-sided trade slightly lowers the Sharpe ratio but the algorithm automatically adjusts by increasing the proportion of times being active. The resulting annualized returns increase. In the year 2022, since most of the time, the futures price is below the spot and we don’t allow longing the futures and shorting the spot trade, the proportion of time the strategy is active is very low.</p>
</div>

<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 7: </span>Portfolio Performance under Different Trading Costs</figcaption><div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1">
<p id="S4.T7.3" class="ltx_p ltx_figure_panel">This table presents the portfolio performance under different trading cost specifications. The fee for spot is 0, 1.5 bps, 3.75 bps, and 5.25 bps for the 4 trading costs specifications. The fee for the futures are 0, 0, 0.54 bp, 1.08 bps for the 4 trading costs specifications.</p></div></div>
</figure>
<div id="S4.SS4.p8" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS4.p8.1" class="ltx_p">Table <a href="#S4.T7" title="Table 7 ‣ 4.4 Data-driven Futures-spot Arbitrage Strategy ‣ 4 Data and Empirical Analysis ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a> further reports the performance of the trading strategy under different trading costs specifications laid out in Table <a href="#S4.T2" title="Table 2 ‣ 4.1 Data ‣ 4 Data and Empirical Analysis ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>. The results from Table <a href="#S4.T6" title="Table 6 ‣ 4.4 Data-driven Futures-spot Arbitrage Strategy ‣ 4 Data and Empirical Analysis ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a> correspond to the last column in Table <a href="#S4.T7" title="Table 7 ‣ 4.4 Data-driven Futures-spot Arbitrage Strategy ‣ 4 Data and Empirical Analysis ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a>. As trading costs increase, our trading strategy dynamically adjusts by lowering the proportion of time being active. The annualized return decreases and annualized standard deviation are of similar magnitude across different trading costs. As a result, SR decreases as trading costs increase. Under no trading cost, we see a Sharpe ratio of 6.72 for BTC and Sharpe ratios above 10 for all other cryptos. This also confirms our theoretical results that when there is no trading cost, any deviation of perpetual price from the no-arbitrage benchmark would be a random-maturity arbitrage opportunity.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS4.p9" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS4.p9.1" class="ltx_p">Comparing Table <a href="#S4.T7" title="Table 7 ‣ 4.4 Data-driven Futures-spot Arbitrage Strategy ‣ 4 Data and Empirical Analysis ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a> with Table <a href="#S4.T5" title="Table 5 ‣ 4.3 Random-maturity Arbitrage Strategy ‣ 4 Data and Empirical Analysis ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>, we find under low and no trading costs, the potential incremental benefits from using a data-driven two-threshold trading rule are much larger compared to higher trading costs. The intuition can be easily illustrated by comparing the empirical real-time trading thresholds in the theory-motivated strategy and the data-driven strategy under low trading costs (Figure <a href="#Sx1.F12" title="Figure 12 ‣ A. Additional figures and tables ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">12</span></a> and Figure <a href="#Sx1.F13" title="Figure 13 ‣ A. Additional figures and tables ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">13</span></a>). With persistent <math id="S4.SS4.p9.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ρ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho</annotation></semantics></math> the data-driven approach can find the optimal close-position threshold corresponding to the level of <math id="S4.SS4.p9.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ρ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho</annotation></semantics></math> while the theory-motivated one is too conservative in setting a close-position threshold equal to 0.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS4.p10" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS4.p10.1" class="ltx_p">There are two sources of trading profit for our trading strategy: (1) the price convergence; (2) the funding rate payment. In Table <a href="#S4.T8" title="Table 8 ‣ 4.4 Data-driven Futures-spot Arbitrage Strategy ‣ 4 Data and Empirical Analysis ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">8</span></a>, we decompose the return to our trading strategy without trading cost into the two sources. We find across different cryptos, the return from price convergence accounts for a larger proportion of the total profit. For BTC, the price convergence accounts for more than <math id="S4.SS4.p10.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2/3" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2/3</annotation></semantics></math> of the profits, and for ETH, it accounts for about <math id="S4.SS4.p10.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="3/4" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">3/4</annotation></semantics></math>. Additionally, the decomposition for the year 2022 generates different patterns, the return due to funding rate plays a much smaller role across different cryptos. This is because the deviation from perpetual to spot is much smaller during the year. The results suggest when more sophisticated arbitrageurs enter the market, the large deviation of perpetual from the spot would be more of an off-equilibrium outcome. As a result, the funding rate payment will also be small.</p>
</div>

<div id="S4.SS4.p11" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS4.p11.1" class="ltx_p">In all, our analysis of the trading strategy demonstrates the profitability of perpetual-spot arbitrage trade. The deviation of the futures to spot can also serve as an important measure for the frictions, trading costs, and limits to arbitrage in the market.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S5" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">5 </span>Explaining Futures-spot Deviation</h2>

<div id="S5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">From Figure <a href="#S4.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ 4.2 Deviations of perpetual futures from no-arbitrage benchmarks ‣ 4 Data and Empirical Analysis ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>, we find strong common comovement of the futures-spot deviation across all crypto assets. We want to understand the factors driving the deviation between futures and spot. Arbitrageurs will only accommodate the demand differences larger than the trading costs. Therefore, the futures-spot gap would be a reflection of the difference in futures demand relative to the spot demand.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p2.1" class="ltx_p">To start off, given the persistent patterns shown in the deviation of perpetual to spot price, we look for persistent sentiment measures that can potentially explain the deviation. We find a fear and greed index from alternative.me can significantly explain the current deviation of futures to spot. A regression of <math id="S5.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ρ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho</annotation></semantics></math> on the fear and greed index yields an <math id="S5.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>R</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R^{2}</annotation></semantics></math> of around 0.3 for BTC and ETH. The website did not publish a detailed methodology for constructing the index. Its major component consists of past price momentum, volatility, social media, and Google trend.</p>
</div>

<div class="ltx_flex_figure ltx_flex_table">

<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 9: </span>Regression of the futures-spot gap against explanatory variables</figcaption><div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1">
<p id="S5.T9.3" class="ltx_p ltx_figure_panel">In this table, we report the regression of <math id="S5.T9.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ρ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho</annotation></semantics></math> on the past four months’ annualized returns (Ret) and fear and greed index (FnG). The left panel reports results for Bitcoin and the right panel reports the results for Ethereum. For each crypto, we consider 3 models: (1) regress <math id="S5.T9.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ρ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho</annotation></semantics></math> on past returns; (2) regress <math id="S5.T9.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ρ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho</annotation></semantics></math> on lagged fear and greed index; (3) regress <math id="S5.T9.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ρ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho</annotation></semantics></math> on both past returns and the fear and greed index. The observations are at a daily frequency. The sample period is 2020-04-30 to 2022-11-13. We start from 2020-04-30 because we need the first 4 months’ data to calculate the past return momentum. The table also reports the R2 of each regression model. We report HAC-robust t-stat in parentheses. <math id="S5.T9.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="*p&lt;.1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">∗</mo><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>&lt;</mo><mn>.1</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">*p&lt;.1</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S5.T9.m6" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="**p&lt;.05" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo rspace="0em">∗</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.222em">∗</mo><mi>p</mi><mo>&lt;</mo><mn>.05</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">**p&lt;.05</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S5.T9.m7" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="***p&lt;.01" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo rspace="0em">∗</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∗</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.222em">∗</mo><mi>p</mi><mo>&lt;</mo><mn>.01</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">***p&lt;.01</annotation></semantics></math></p></div></div>
</figure>
<div id="S5.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p3.1" class="ltx_p">To open up this black box, we calculate past return momentum and volatility. We find that past return momentum can explain a larger proportion of the futures spot deviation. After controlling for the past return, the incremental explanatory power from the fear and greed index is very small. We find that a regression of <math id="S5.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ρ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho</annotation></semantics></math> on the past four months’ average return yields an <math id="S5.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>R</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R^{2}</annotation></semantics></math> over <math id="S5.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="50\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>50</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">50\%</annotation></semantics></math> for both BTC and ETH. We find similar robust patterns using past returns ranging from 1 month to 12 months.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Table <a href="#S5.T9" title="Table 9 ‣ 5 Explaining Futures-spot Deviation ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">9</span></a> reports the regression results of <math id="S5.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ρ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho</annotation></semantics></math> on past returns, fear and greed index, and both for BTC and ETH. The regression coefficient on past returns is positive and highly significant. This means when the past return is high, the futures will have more positive deviation against the spot. In other words, when past return is high, the demand for futures relative to the spot is also likely to be high so that after the arbitrageurs accommodate the demand outside the trading cost, the residual demand still manifests itself through perpetual-spot deviation.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p5.1" class="ltx_p"><cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu and Tsyvinski (2021)</a></cite> document a significant time-series momentum pattern in the crypto market. Given the fact that positive past returns would lead to a positive gap between the futures and the spot, it is worth examining further whether the time-series momentum phenomenon is caused by the margin trading and price pressure from the perpetual futures market. We leave this as an open question for later papers.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p6.1" class="ltx_p">We find the volatility does not significantly covary with the futures and spot deviation. It indicates volatility does not covary with the persistent sentiment in the perpetual futures market. Also, betting on the convergence of futures and spot is a generalized risk-free arbitrage opportunity. Even with high volatility, the trade is still risk-free in a generalized sense. Therefore, the traditional argument behind limits to arbitrage would not apply here. (<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">Shleifer and Vishny (1997)</a></cite>).</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.p7" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p7.1" class="ltx_p">To recap, the pre-condition for the gap between futures and the spot to occur is the existence of trading costs for arbitrageurs. The arbitrage trading will accommodate all the demand in the futures until the price deviation lies within a trading cost bound. The relative sentiment of futures compared to the spot will still manifest itself in the deviation of futures price to the spot. This relative sentiment can be significantly explained by past returns. Since there is a significant market factor explaining the time-series comovement of all the cryptos, the relative sentiment of futures to spot will also highly comove with each other. As a result, we observe a significant common factor in crypto future-spot deviations.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S6" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">6 </span>Conclusions</h2>

<div id="S6.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Perpetual futures play important role in crypto trades. Understanding the fundamental mechanism of the financial derivative is crucial for apprehending the speculation and hedging dynamics in this fast-evolving arena. We provide a comprehensive analysis of the arbitrage and funding rate payment mechanisms behind perpetual futures pricing.</p>
</div>
<div id="S6.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.p2.1" class="ltx_p">In a frictionless world, arbitrageurs will trade the perpetual futures such that there is a constant relationship between the future price and the spot. In the presence of trading costs, the deviation of the futures price to the spot would lie within a bound.</p>
</div>
<div id="S6.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Motivated by the theory, we then empirically characterize the comovement of the futures-spot spread across different cryptos and implement both a theory-motivated arbitrage strategy and a data-driven arbitrage strategy. We find both strategies deliver sizable SRs across different trading cost specifications. The evidence supports our theoretical argument that perpetual-spot spreads beyond the trading costs would be a generalized risk-free arbitrage opportunity.</p>
</div>
<div id="S6.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Last but not least, we provide an explanation for the common comovement in futures-spot spread across different crypto-currencies: the arbitrageurs can only accommodate the demand in the market if the price deviation is larger than the trading costs. So the overall sentiment in the futures market relative to the spot will manifest itself in the spread. We find empirically that past return momentum can explain a significant amount of time-series variation in the futures-spot spread.</p>
</div>
<div class="ltx_pagination ltx_role_newpage"></div>
<div class="ltx_pagination ltx_role_newpage"></div>
</section>

<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 7: </span>Trading view of BTC perpetual futures on Binance</figcaption><div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1">
<p id="Sx1.F7.2" class="ltx_p ltx_figure_panel">This figure presents the perpetual futures trading view on Binance. The key information includes futures price (Mark), spot price (Index), real-time funding rate based on the rolling average of the past 8 hours’ observations, and countdown toward funding rate payment (Funding / Countdown) (illustrated with a red rectangle). In this example, futures are trading at a lower price than the spot. The funding rate is negative and is to be paid in 1 hour and 12 minutes.</p></div></div>

<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 8: </span>Trading costs tiers for the spot market</figcaption><div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1">
<p id="Sx1.F8.2" class="ltx_p ltx_figure_panel">This figure presents the trading costs tiers for the crypto spot market from Binance: <a href="https://www.binance.com/en/fee/trading" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">https://www.binance.com/en/fee/trading</a>. Our high, medium, and low trading cost specification corresponds to VIP 1, VIP 5, and VIP 8 tiers as illustrated with red rectangles in the picture. The 30-day trading volume requirements for VIP 1, 5, and 8 are 1 million, 150 million, and 2 billion respectively in the spot market. We consider the trading costs for makers as institutions typically trade maker orders. Binance offers a temporary discount for VIP 4-8 to have the same trading cost as VIP 9. We consider the non-discounted trading costs to make the comparison more reliable and fair.</p></div></div>
</figure>

<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 9: </span>Trading costs tiers for the perp market</figcaption><div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1">
<p id="Sx1.F9.2" class="ltx_p ltx_figure_panel">This figure presents the trading costs tiers for the crypto perpetual market from Binance: <a href="https://www.binance.com/en/fee/trading" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">https://www.binance.com/en/fee/trading</a>. Our high, medium, and low trading cost specification corresponds to VIP 1, VIP 5, and VIP 8 tiers as illustrated with red rectangles in the picture. The 30-day trading volume requirements for VIP 1, 5, and 8 are 15 million, 1 billion, and 12.5 billion respectively in the perpetual market. We consider the trading costs for makers as institutions typically trade maker orders.</p></div></div>
</figure>
<figure id="Sx1.F10" class="ltx_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1"><img src="2212.06888v2/figures/exchanges_fr_ethereum.png" id="Sx1.F10.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_figure_panel ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/186;" width="476" height="186" alt="Refer to caption"></div></div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 10: </span>Ether annualized funding rate across exchanges</figcaption><div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1">
<p id="Sx1.F10.2" class="ltx_p ltx_figure_panel">The figure presents the 7-day moving average annualized funding rate for Ether (ETH) across exchanges. The data is obtained from glassnode, an analytics platform. The data covers two major market turbulences: the COVID stock market crash from February to April 2020, and the FTX insolvency in November 2022. The FTX collapse led to significant negative funding rates on all solvent exchanges, thus the perpetual future prices were lower than the spot prices on the solvent exchanges. Vice versa on the insolvent FTX. The funding rates become more volatile after the event, indicating increased uncertainty for the market participants.</p></div></div>
</figure>
<figure id="Sx1.F11" class="ltx_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2212.06888v2/interest_rate.svg" id="Sx1.F11.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_figure_panel ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/234;" width="476" height="234"></object></div></div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 11: </span>Annualized interest rate from Aave</figcaption><div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1">
<p id="Sx1.F11.2" class="ltx_p ltx_figure_panel">This figure presents the daily supply and borrowing rate from Aave. We consider three stablecoins: USDT, USDC, and DAI. Each day, we take the average interest rate of the 3 crypto stablecoins to get the proxy for the risk-free funding rate of the arbitrageurs. The averaging removes the idiosyncratic noise in borrowing and supply in individual stablecoins. The sample period is from 2020-01-08 to 2022-11-13.</p></div></div>
</figure>
<figure id="Sx1.F12" class="ltx_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1"><img src="2212.06888v2/figures/figure_trading_theory.png" id="Sx1.F12.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_figure_panel ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:476/565;" width="476" height="565" alt="Refer to caption"></div></div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 12: </span>Trading Strategy Visualization: Random-maturity Arbitrage</figcaption><div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1">
<p id="Sx1.F12.2" class="ltx_p ltx_figure_panel">This figure presents the random-maturity arbitrage strategy motivated by the theory. The orange, green and purple lines correspond to the open-position threshold under high, medium, and low trading costs. The red line represents the close-position threshold.</p></div></div>
</figure>
<figure id="Sx1.F13" class="ltx_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1"><img src="2212.06888v2/figures/figure_trading_1.png" id="Sx1.F13.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_figure_panel ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:476/565;" width="476" height="565" alt="Refer to caption"></div></div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 13: </span>Trading Strategy Visualization: No Trading Costs</figcaption><div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1">
<p id="Sx1.F13.2" class="ltx_p ltx_figure_panel">This figure presents the real-time trading thresholds under no trading costs. The orange line is the open-position threshold and the red line is the close-position threshold. The trading thresholds are determined based on the adjusted SR from the past 6 months.</p></div></div>
</figure>
<figure id="Sx1.F14" class="ltx_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure">
