<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1">
<p id="Sx1.F14.2" class="ltx_p ltx_figure_panel">This figure presents the real-time trading thresholds under low trading costs (2.25 bps for spot trading and 0.18 bp for futures trading). The orange line is the open-position threshold and the red line is the close-position threshold. The trading thresholds are determined based on the adjusted SR from the past 6 months.</p></div></div>
</figure>
<figure id="Sx1.F15" class="ltx_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1"><img src="2212.06888v2/figures/figure_trading_3.png" id="Sx1.F15.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_figure_panel ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:476/565;" width="476" height="565" alt="Refer to caption"></div></div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 15: </span>Trading Strategy Visualization: Medium Trading Costs</figcaption><div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1">
<p id="Sx1.F15.2" class="ltx_p ltx_figure_panel">This figure presents the real-time trading thresholds under medium trading costs (4.5 bps for spot trading and 0.72 bp for futures trading). The orange line is the open-position threshold and the red line is the close-position threshold. The trading thresholds are determined based on the adjusted SR from the past 6 months.</p></div></div>
</figure>
<figure id="Sx1.F16" class="ltx_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1"><img src="2212.06888v2/figures/figure_trading_4.png" id="Sx1.F16.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_figure_panel ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:476/565;" width="476" height="565" alt="Refer to caption"></div></div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 16: </span>Trading Strategy Visualization: High Trading Costs</figcaption><div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1">
<p id="Sx1.F16.2" class="ltx_p ltx_figure_panel">This figure presents the real-time trading thresholds under high trading costs (6.75 bps for spot trading and 1.44 bps for futures trading). The orange line is the open-position threshold and the red line is the close-position threshold. The trading thresholds are determined based on the adjusted SR from the past 6 months.</p></div></div>
</figure>
<div class="ltx_pagination ltx_role_newpage"></div>
</section>
<section id="Sx2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section">B. High-frequency event study of funding rate payment</h2>

<div id="Sx2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this part, we provide a high-frequency event study around the funding rate payment time. We hope to further understand the microstructure effect of the funding rate mechanism on perpetual futures pricing. We obtain 1-min BTC, ETH, and DOGE price data from Kaiko. We then calculate the return from a strategy that taps into the funding rate payment with a window of -4 hours and +4 hours around the funding rate payment. When the funding rate is positive, we stay on the short side of the perpetual futures to receive the funding rate and long the spot to hedge the risk. When the funding rate is negative, we do the trade in the opposite direction.</p>
</div>
<div id="Sx2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Figure <a href="#Sx2.F17" title="Figure 17 ‣ B. High-frequency event study of funding rate payment ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">17</span></a> presents the average ex-funding-rate cumulative returns of such a strategy around the time of funding rate payment for BTC, ETH, and DOGE. We see when the funding rate is positive, there is a significant price drop. This reflects the efficiency of the market. When traders observe almost certain positive funding rate payments. They have incentives to short the futures and long the spot. This behavior results in a large decline in spot-perpetual return, which offsets the profits from gaining the funding rate.</p>
</div>
<div id="Sx2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">On the other hand, we observe less-significant price drops around negative funding rate payments. This can be due to 2 reasons: (1) in our sample, only around 15% of the sample has a negative funding rate and the magnitude is smaller than the positive funding rate. A small sample would result in noisy estimates making it more difficult to discover the patterns in the positive case. (2) To implement the arbitrage strategy, the traders need to long the futures and short the spot. However, the infrastructure for shorting the spot is not well-developed for the crypto spot market. Trading in the futures market alone would expose the traders to too much risk. Because of these limits to arbitrage, we observe a more muted price decline around negative funding rate payments.</p>
</div>
<div id="Sx2.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx2.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Even if the price shows a large decline at high-frequency, it is worth inspecting how much trading profit is left from exploiting the funding rate payment. We implement a high-frequency funding rate arbitrage strategy. Five minutes before the funding rate payment, we are going to open the position in the futures and spot market. We close the position 5 minutes after the funding rate payment.</p>
</div>
<div id="Sx2.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx2.p5.1" class="ltx_p">We found that the average one-time return from implementing the strategy is about 1.5 bps, which sums up to 16.4% per year. However, implementing the strategy requires round-trip trading in the spot market which has a total trading cost of 3 bps even under low trading cost specification. Therefore after accounting for trading costs, the trading profits will be attenuated. The price movement in perpetual and spot attenuates about <math id="Sx2.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\frac{1}{3}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>3</mn></mfrac><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{1}{3}</annotation></semantics></math> of the original profits from receiving the funding rate across the three different cryptos.</p>
</div>
<figure id="Sx2.F17" class="ltx_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2212.06888v2/funding_rate_event_study-eps-converted-to.svg" id="Sx2.F17.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_figure_panel ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:476/409;" width="476" height="409"></object></div></div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 17: </span>High-frequency Event Study around the Funding Rate Payment time for BTC, ETH, and DOGE</figcaption><div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1">
<p id="Sx2.F17.2" class="ltx_p ltx_figure_panel">This figure shows cumulative returns to strategies that try to exploit the funding rate payment at the 1-minute frequency for BTC, ETH, and DOGE. The strategies returns reported in the figure do not include the funding rate payment, similar to the ex-dividend returns to stock around the dividend payment. The blue line shows cumulative return to a strategy that shorts the futures and longs the spot when the funding rate is positive. The orange line shows cumulative return to a strategy that longs the futures and shorts the spot when the funding rate is negative.</p></div></div>
</figure>
</section>
</article>
